      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>

      <content name="FullSummary">What is <span class="qt0">menstruation</span>?<p><span class="qt0">Menstruation</span>, also called a period, is normal vaginal bleeding that happens as part of the monthly cycle in women and girls. Every month, the body prepares for pregnancy. If pregnancy does not happen, the uterus (womb) sheds its lining. This blood and tissue leave the body through the vagina.</p>What is the <span class="qt0">menstrual</span> cycle?<p>The <span class="qt0">menstrual</span> cycle is the monthly process the body goes through to prepare for pregnancy. It is counted from the first day of one period to the first day of the next. Most <span class="qt0">menstrual</span> cycles last about 28 days, but cycles can be shorter or longer and still be normal.</p>When will my period start?<p>Most girls start having a period between ages 9 and 15, but some may start earlier or later. A period usually lasts three to seven days and can be light or heavy. It may take a few years to become regular.</p><p>Your period may change during times that affect hormones, such as after childbirth or while breastfeeding. Periods usually continue until menopause, which most often happens between ages 45 and 55.</p>What are the symptoms of <span class="qt0">menstruation</span>?<p>In addition to vaginal bleeding, you may have:</p><ul><li>Cramping pain in the lower abdomen (belly) or pelvis</li><li>Lower back pain</li><li>Bloating</li><li>Sore breasts</li><li>Food cravings</li><li>Mood swings or irritability</li><li>Headaches or fatigue</li></ul><p>Premenstrual syndrome (PMS) is a group of physical and emotional symptoms that can happen in the days before a period starts. Many women have some PMS symptoms, which usually go away after their period begins.</p><p>Many women and girls use <span class="qt0">menstrual</span> products such as pads, tampons, <span class="qt0">menstrual</span> cups, or period underwear to manage bleeding during their period. Changing or cleaning these products often helps you stay comfortable and clean.</p>What are <span class="qt0">menstrual</span> irregularities?<p><span class="qt0">Menstrual</span> irregularities are changes in the usual <span class="qt0">menstrual</span> cycle. These may include missed periods, irregular periods, or heavy bleeding. Common <span class="qt0">menstrual</span> irregularities include:</p><ul><li>Amenorrhea means not having a period.</li><li>Oligomenorrhea means having periods that happen less often.</li><li>Menorrhagia means very heavy <span class="qt0">menstrual</span> bleeding.</li><li>Prolonged <span class="qt0">menstrual</span> bleeding occurs when periods regularly last longer than 8 days.</li><li>Dysmenorrhea refers to painful periods that may include severe cramps.</li></ul><p>Keep track of your period each month. This can help you understand your usual cycle, know when to expect your next period, and notice changes.</p><p>Talk with your health care provider if you notice major changes in your <span class="qt0">menstrual</span> cycle, very heavy bleeding, or severe pain. These may be signs of other health problems that need treatment.</p><p>NIH: National Institute of Child Health and Human Development</p></content>

    <document rank="1" url="https://medlineplus.gov/depression.html">
      <content name="title">Depression</content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Dysthymic Disorder</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Clinical depression</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Major depressive disorder</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Unipolar depression</content>
      <content name="FullSummary">What is depression?<p>Depression is more than a feeling of being sad or irritable for a few days. It's a serious mood disorder. As one of the most common mental disorders in the United States, depression can affect how you think, feel, and your everyday life. You may not know why you feel this way, but even basic daily activities such as sleeping, eating, or working may become difficult. Depression often needs long-term treatment but getting help at the earliest sign of a problem can help manage your symptoms.</p>What are the different types of depression?<p>The most common types of depression are major depression and persistent depressive disorder.</p><ul><li>Major depression symptoms include a depressed mood or a loss of interest. Symptoms affect your daily activities and last for at least two weeks.</li><li>Persistent depressive disorder (also called dysthymia or dysthymic disorder) has less severe depressive symptoms, but they last longer, usually for at least two years.</li></ul><p>Other types of depression can include:</p><ul><li>Seasonal affective disorder comes and goes with the seasons. It usually starts in late fall and early winter and goes away during the spring and summer.</li><li>Bipolar disorder is sometimes called manic depression. This mood disorder can cause intense mood swings.</li><li>Depression with symptoms of psychosis is a severe form of depression that also has delusions (false beliefs) or hallucinations (seeing, hearing, or feeling something that isn't there).</li></ul>What causes depression?<p>There are a variety of things that may cause depression, including genetic, biological, environmental, and psychological factors. Depression can happen at any age and can affect anyone, but it's more common in women. This is often due to the physical and hormonal changes that women have during <span class="qt0">menstruation</span>, pregnancy, the postpartum period, and menopause. Other mental disorders or chronic medical conditions such as diabetes, cancer, or heart disease may occur with depression. This may make the chronic condition or depression worse.</p><p>In some cases, there is no clear cause for depression.</p>Who is at risk of depression?<p>You may be at a higher risk of depression if you have a close relative who has it or another mental health disorder. Going through trauma or stressful life events may raise your risk even more.</p>What are the symptoms of depression?<p>Depression doesn't look the same on everyone. The type and number of symptoms of depression can vary and don't always appear like sadness. Depression may affect you differently based on your:</p><ul><li>Age. The symptoms of depression may be different in a child, who may appear more irritable than sad. Teens may act out or have excessive sleepiness. The symptoms for an older adult may not be as obvious as other age groups.</li><li>Sex. Men often show symptoms and coping behaviors differently than women. Rather than sad, men may appear angry or irritable.</li><li>Medical conditions. Some medicines and medical conditions may cause symptoms that look like depression. Chronic conditions may make depression worse.</li></ul><p>Symptoms of depression are ongoing and affect your day-to-day life. They can include:</p><ul><li>Feeling sad or "empty"</li><li>Losing interest in favorite activities</li><li>Overeating, or not wanting to eat at all</li><li>Sleeping too much, or not enough</li><li>Feeling very tired</li><li>Feeling hopeless, irritable, anxious, or guilty</li><li>Having aches and pains, headaches, cramps, or digestive problems</li><li>Having thoughts of death or suicide</li><li>Changing moods or behaviors</li><li>Increasing use of alcohol or drugs</li><li>Isolating from family and friends</li></ul>How is depression diagnosed?<p>If you think you have depression, talk to your health care provider or a mental health provider. To be diagnosed with depression, your provider may use many tools:</p><ul><li>A medical history will include asking about your symptoms and family history. To be diagnosed with depression, your symptoms must occur most of the day, nearly every day, for at least two weeks. One of the symptoms must be a depressed mood or a loss of interest in most activities.</li><li>Medical tests may be done to rule out other medical conditions. Certain medicines and medical conditions (such as viruses or thyroid disorders) may cause symptoms like depression.</li><li>A physical exam to make sure another issue isn't causing your symptoms.</li><li>A mental health evaluation by your provider or a mental health provider.</li></ul>What are the treatments for depression?<p>Depression may need long-term treatment. Most treatments include medicines and/or psychotherapy (talk therapy):</p><ul><li>Medicines such as antidepressants may help control your symptoms. You may need to try several medicines to find which works best for you. Medicine may take time to work and can have side effects. Don't stop taking your medicine without first talking with your provider. Contact your provider if you have any concerns about side effects from the medicine.</li><li>Psychotherapy (talk therapy) under the care of a mental health provider can help you recognize and change troubling emotions, thoughts, and behaviors. This may be done one-on-one or in a group setting. It can give you and your family support, education, skills, and coping strategies.</li><li>Light therapy has been shown to be effective for seasonal affective disorder (SAD).</li><li>Other treatments options may be considered if treatment isn't working or if depression is severe. These may include:
	<ul><li>Electroconvulsive therapy (ECT) is a brain stimulation procedure that uses a mild electric current when you are under general anesthesia. ECT is most often used for severe depression that is not getting better with other treatments.</li><li>Repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS) is a brain stimulation procedure that uses magnetic waves to relieve depression. It's not as powerful as ECT, but with rTMS, you don't need anesthesia. It also has a low risk of negative effects on your memory and thinking.</li></ul>
</li></ul>Can depression be prevented?<p>Most cases of depression can't be prevented, but healthy lifestyle changes can have long-term benefits for your mental health. These can include:</p><ul><li>Getting regular exercise</li><li>Having a consistent sleep schedule</li><li>Controlling stress</li></ul><p>If you, or someone you love is depressed, see your provider or a mental health provider. It's important to get treatment at the earliest sign of a problem.</p><p>If you or someone you know has thoughts of hurting themselves or attempting suicide, get help right away. If it is an emergency, dial 911.</p><p>NIH: National Institute of Mental Health</p></content>

      <content name="title">Migraine</content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Vascular Headache</content>
      <content name="FullSummary">What are migraines?<p>Migraines are a recurring type of headache. They cause moderate to severe pain that is throbbing or pulsing. The pain is often on one side of your head. You may also have other symptoms, such as nausea and weakness. You may be sensitive to light and sound.</p>What causes migraines?<p>Researchers believe that migraine has a genetic cause. There are also a number of factors that can trigger a migraine. These factors vary from person to person, and they include:</p><ul><li>Stress</li><li>Anxiety</li><li>Hormonal changes in women</li><li>Bright or flashing lights</li><li>Loud noises</li><li>Strong smells</li><li>Medicines</li><li>Too much or not enough sleep</li><li>Sudden changes in weather or environment</li><li>Overexertion (too much physical activity)</li><li>Tobacco</li><li>Caffeine or caffeine withdrawal</li><li>Skipped meals</li><li>Medication overuse (taking medicine for migraines too often)</li></ul><p>Some people have found that certain foods or ingredients can trigger headaches, especially when they are combined with other triggers. These foods and ingredients include:</p><ul><li>Alcohol</li><li>Chocolate</li><li>Aged cheeses</li><li>Monosodium glutamate (MSG)</li><li>Some fruits and nuts</li><li>Fermented or pickled goods</li><li>Yeast</li><li>Cured or processed meats</li></ul>Who is at risk for migraines?<p>About 12% of Americans get migraines. They can affect anyone, but you are more likely to have them if you:</p><ul><li>Are a woman. Women are three times more likely than men to get migraines.</li><li>Have a family history of migraines. Most people with migraines have family members who have migraines.</li><li>Have other medical conditions, such as depression, anxiety, bipolar disorder, sleep disorders, and epilepsy.</li></ul>What are the symptoms of migraines?<p>There are four different phases of migraines. You may not always go through every phase each time you have a migraine.:</p><ul><li>Prodome. This phase starts up to 24 hours before you get the migraine. You have early signs and symptoms, such as food cravings, unexplained mood changes, uncontrollable yawning, fluid retention, and increased urination.</li><li>Aura. If you have this phase, you might see flashing or bright lights or zig-zag lines. You may have muscle weakness or feel like you are being touched or grabbed. An aura can happen just before or during a migraine.</li><li>Headache. A migraine usually starts gradually and then becomes more severe. It typically causes throbbing or pulsing pain, which is often on one side of your head. But sometimes you can have a migraine without a headache. Other migraine symptoms may include</li><ul><li>Increased sensitivity to light, noise, and odors</li><li>Nausea and vomiting</li><li>Worsened pain when you move, cough, or sneeze</li></ul><li>Postdrome (following the headache). You may feel exhausted, weak, and confused after a migraine. This can last up to a day.</li></ul><p>Migraines are more common in the morning; people often wake up with them. Some people have migraines at predictable times, such as before <span class="qt0">menstruation</span> or on weekends following a stressful week of work.</p>How are migraines diagnosed?<p>To make a diagnosis, your health care provider will:</p><ul><li>Take your medical history</li><li>Ask about your symptoms</li><li>Do a physical and neurological exam</li></ul><p>An important part of diagnosing migraines is to rule out other medical conditions which could be causing the symptoms. So you may also have blood tests, an MRI or CT scan, or other tests.</p>How are migraines treated?<p>There is no cure for migraines. Treatment focuses on relieving symptoms and preventing additional attacks.</p><p>There are different types of medicines to relieve symptoms. They include triptan drugs, ergotamine drugs, and pain relievers. The sooner you take the medicine, the more effective it is.</p><p>There are also other things you can do to feel better:</p><ul><li>Resting with your eyes closed in a quiet, darkened room</li><li>Placing a cool cloth or ice pack on your forehead</li><li>Drinking fluids</li></ul><p>There are some lifestyle changes you can make to prevent migraines:</p><ul><li>Stress management strategies, such as exercise, relaxation techniques, and biofeedback, may reduce the number and severity of migraines. Biofeedback uses electronic devices to teach you to control certain body functions, such as your heartbeat, blood pressure, and muscle tension.</li><li>Make a log of what seems to trigger your migraines. You can learn what you need to avoid, such as certain foods and medicines. It also help you figure out what you should do, such as establishing a consistent sleep schedule and eating regular meals.</li><li>Hormone therapy may help some women whose migraines seem to be linked to their <span class="qt0">menstrual</span> cycle</li><li>If you have obesity, losing weight may also be helpful</li></ul><p>If you have frequent or severe migraines, you may need to take medicines to prevent further attacks. Talk with your health care provider about which drug would be right for you.</p><p>Certain natural treatments, such as riboflavin (vitamin B2) and coenzyme Q10, may help prevent migraines. If your magnesium level is low, you can try taking magnesium. There is also an herb, butterbur, which some people take to prevent migraines. But butterbur may not be safe for long-term use. Always check with your health care provider before taking any supplements.</p><p>NIH: National Institute of Neurological Disorders and Stroke</p></content>

    <document rank="3" url="https://medlineplus.gov/ovariandisorders.html">
      <content name="title">Ovarian Disorders</content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Ovarian Insufficiency</content>
      <content name="FullSummary">What are ovaries?<p>The ovaries are a pair of female reproductive glands that make eggs and female hormones. Women have one ovary on each side of the uterus (where a fetus grows during pregnancy). Each ovary is about the size and shape of an almond.</p><p>Ovaries play a role in <span class="qt0">menstruation</span>, pregnancy, and menopause.  Your ovaries:</p><ul><li>Produce and store eggs that are released during ovulation (when an egg leaves the ovary and travels into the fallopian tube). If a sperm fertilizes the egg, you can become pregnant.</li><li>Make the female hormones estrogen and progesterone.</li><li>Stop making those hormones and releasing eggs during menopause.</li></ul><p>Some medical problems can affect the ovaries. These can cause various symptoms, and some ovarian disorders may need prompt treatment.</p>What are the types of ovarian disorders?<p>Some problems that can happen with the ovaries can include:</p><ul><li>Ovarian cancer is when a cancerous tumor forms in the tissues of an ovary.</li><li>Ovarian cysts are fluid-filled sacs in or on an ovary.</li><li>Polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) is a set of symptoms related to an imbalance of hormones.</li><li>Primary ovarian insufficiency is when your ovaries stop working before age 40.</li><li>Ovarian torsion is a twisting of the ovary.</li><li>Endometriosis is when tissue like the lining in your uterus grows in other places in your body. It may affect the ovaries, fallopian tubes, and tissue lining the pelvis.</li><li>Pelvic inflammatory disease is an infection and inflammation of the uterus, ovaries, and other female reproductive organs.</li><li>Ovarian tumors.</li></ul>What causes ovarian disorders?<p>Ovarian disorders can happen for different reasons depending on the condition. Sometimes the cause is unknown.</p>What are the symptoms of ovarian disorders?<p>Your symptoms may be different, depending on the problem with your ovaries. Some ovarian disorders, such as ovarian cysts, may cause few or even no symptoms. Other disorders may cause more severe symptoms. Symptoms can include:</p><ul><li>Pelvic pain, which often happens during your period</li><li>Nausea or diarrhea</li><li>Vaginal bleeding that is between periods, very heavy, or longer than usual</li><li>Vaginal discharge</li><li>Painful <span class="qt0">menstrual</span> cramps</li></ul>How are ovarian disorders diagnosed?<p>To find out if you have a problem with your ovaries, your health care provider:</p><ul><li>Will ask about your medical history, including your symptoms</li><li>Will ask about your family health history</li><li>Will do a physical exam, including a pelvic exam</li><li>May order imaging tests, or blood tests</li></ul>What are the treatments for ovarian disorders?<p>Treatment depends on the ovarian disorder, your symptoms, overall health, and plans for pregnancy. Treatment can include medicines, such as pain relievers or hormonal birth control, lifestyle changes to reduce symptoms, or sometimes surgery. Ovarian cancer may require surgery, chemotherapy, or other targeted therapy.</p></content>

    <document rank="4" url="https://medlineplus.gov/periodpain.html">
      <content name="title">Period Pain</content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Dysmenorrhea</content>
      <content name="altTitle"><span class="qt0">Menstrual</span> Cramps</content>
      <content name="altTitle"><span class="qt0">Menstrual</span> pain</content>
      <content name="FullSummary">What are painful periods?<p><span class="qt0">Menstruation</span>, or period, is normal vaginal bleeding that happens as part of a woman's monthly cycle. Many women have painful periods, also called dysmenorrhea. The pain is most often <span class="qt0">menstrual</span> cramps, which are a throbbing, cramping pain in your lower abdomen. You may also have other symptoms, such as lower back pain, nausea, diarrhea, and headaches. Period pain is not the same as premenstrual syndrome (PMS). PMS causes many different symptoms, including weight gain, bloating, irritability, and fatigue. PMS often starts one to two weeks before your period starts.</p>What causes painful periods?<p>There are two types of dysmenorrhea: primary and secondary. Each type has different causes.</p><p>Primary dysmenorrhea is the most common kind of period pain. It is period pain that is not caused by another condition. The cause is usually having too many prostaglandins, which are chemicals that your uterus makes. These chemicals make the muscles of your uterus tighten and relax, and this causes the cramps.</p><p>The pain can start a day or two before your period. It normally lasts for a few days, though in some women it can last longer.</p><p>You usually first start having period pain when you are younger, just after you begin getting periods. Often, as you get older, you have less pain. The pain may also get better after you have given birth.</p><p>Secondary dysmenorrhea often starts later in life. It is caused by conditions that affect your uterus or other reproductive organs, such as endometriosis and uterine fibroids. This kind of pain often gets worse over time. It may begin before your period starts and continue after your period ends.</p>What can I do about period pain?<p>To help ease your period pain, you can try:</p><ul><li>Using a heating pad or hot water bottle on your lower abdomen</li><li>Getting some exercise</li><li>Taking a hot bath</li><li>Doing relaxation techniques, including yoga and meditation</li></ul><p>You might also try taking over-the-counter pain relievers such as nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs). NSAIDs include ibuprofen and naproxen. Besides relieving pain, NSAIDs reduce the amount of prostaglandins that your uterus makes and lessen their effects.  This helps to lessen the cramps. You can take NSAIDs when you first have symptoms, or when your period starts. You can keep taking them for a few days. You should not take NSAIDS if you have ulcers or other stomach problems, bleeding problems, or liver disease. You should also not take them if you are allergic to aspirin. Always check with your health care provider if you are not sure whether or not you should take NSAIDs.</p><p>It may also help to get enough rest and avoid using alcohol and tobacco.</p>When should I get medical help for my period pain?<p>For many women, some pain during your period is normal. However, you should contact your health care provider if:</p><ul><li>NSAIDs and self-care measures don't help, and the pain interferes with your life</li><li>Your cramps suddenly get worse</li><li>You are over 25 and you get severe cramps for the first time</li><li>You have a fever with your period pain</li><li>You have the pain even when you are not getting your period</li></ul>How is the cause of severe period pain diagnosed?<p>To diagnose severe period pain, your health care provider will ask you about your medical history and do a pelvic exam. You may also have an ultrasound or other imaging test. If your health care provider thinks you have secondary dysmenorrhea, you might have laparoscopy. It is a surgery that lets your health care provider look inside your body.</p>What are treatments for severe period pain?<p>If your period pain is primary dysmenorrhea and you need medical treatment, your health care provider might suggest using hormonal birth control, such as the pill, patch, ring, or IUD. Another treatment option might be prescription pain relievers.</p><p>If you have secondary dysmenorrhea, your treatment depends upon the condition that is causing the problem. In some cases, you may need surgery.</p></content>
